items.originalTitle: Zelensky Says Ukraine Sank Russian Warship at Naval Base in Libya
items.author: Tiago Ventura
items.title: Zelensky Says Ukraine Sank Russian Warship at Naval Base in Libya
items.summary: Vantor satellite image shows a vessel partly visible in the water beside a pier in Benghazi. Scattered debris and darkened areas are visible along the pier on Nov. 22, 2026. —Vantor—Getty Images Ukraine sank a Russian warship moored at a port in Libya using naval drones, said Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. Forces deployed seven Ukrainian-made drones that struck and sank the Russian corvette Mercury, which was carrying a combat helicopter, Zelensky said Monday morning. A second ship, the Russian container carrier MV ANGARA, which Zelensky said was being used to “transport weapons,” was also hit. Footage released by Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense appeared to show sea drones speeding toward the warship—one of the newest in Russia's fleet—before it erupted into a giant ball of flames. The Mercury was commissioned a year after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and incorporates some of Moscow’s latest shipbuilding technology, Russian state news agency TASS reported when the ship joined the fleet in May 2023. Russia’s Defense Ministry has yet to comment on the attack. Zelensky hailed the sinking of the warship as an example of an “exemplary Ukrainian operation in response to Russia’s war.” Later Monday morning, Zelensky made a virtual appearance at the NATO Parliamentary Assembly in Berlin, where peace opportunities for Ukraine and suspected Russian violations of NATO airspace were top of the agenda. “Today, Russia can feel our response all the way from western Siberia, where its oil refiners are burning, to the coast of Libya, where its warships are sinking,” Zelensky said as he addressed attendees. “We have offered Russia steps to reduce the fighting dozens, dozens of times, and we have never been the ones. But, unfortunately Russia gives us no peaceful response.” The strikes against the corvette, conducted around 2,400 kilometers (1,500 miles) from the front line in Ukraine, underscore Kyiv's long-range strike capabilities. The Mercury had been in the port of Benghazi to refuel under a maritime cooperation agreement before its planned return to Russia, according to Libya’s Government of National Stability (GNS). In the wake of the strikes, the GNS, which controls eastern Libya and has a longstanding military relationship with Russia, said it had filed an official complaint with the U.N. Secretary-General and Security Council over threats to maritime security, arguing that the country is not a party to the Russia-Ukraine war. The U.N. Support Mission in Libya called for an “immediate, independent, and transparent investigation,” offered U.N. assistance, and warned against drawing Libya into a wider confrontation. U.S.-mediated talks between Russian and Ukrainian delegations resumed earlier this month after a nine-month hiatus, but there is still no clear pathway to peace. President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin, and Chinese President Xi Jinping met for a historic sit-down at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit last week. Trump and Putin had a one-on-one conversation on the sidelines beforehand, but all communications failed to produce any meaningful progress toward ending the Russia-Ukraine war. Russian cargo vessel hit by drone in Baltic Sea The strike in Libya followed a separate drone attack on a Russian cargo vessel in the eastern Gulf of Finland on Saturday, according to Finland's Ministry of Defence. The Sparta II had been bound for Russia's Baltic exclave of Kaliningrad when it was struck Saturday morning. The vessel caught fire and drifted into Finnish territorial waters before being towed out Sunday by a Russian rescue vessel, following a Finnish-led response involving Estonia and Russia. While Kyiv has not claimed responsibility for the attack, Aki-Mauri Huhtinen, director of communications for the Finnish Defense Forces, told local media “it is likely that Ukraine” was behind the strike. TIME has reached out to Ukraine's Defense Ministry for comment. The Kremlin described the attack on the Russia bulk carrier as escalating tensions in international waters. "All coastal countries are certainly concerned about this. This is very dangerous. It is escalating tensions in the region,” said Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov, according to TASS . The U.S. Treasury previously sanctioned the Sparta II in 2022, alleging that the vessel was linked to Russian military logistics company Oboronlogistika. NATO “will defend every inch of Polish territory,” says Rutte NATO chief Mark Rutte pledged Saturday that the alliance would “defend every inch of Polish territory,” speaking to reporters in Warsaw a day after two Russian missiles and a drone crashed in Polish territory. items.author: Chad de Guzman
items.title: Scott Olson—Getty Images
items.summary: A sign identifying the facility sits inside a fence surrounding the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, on Nov. 19, 2026. The U.S. Army said it is pushing through with the controlled detonation of more than five dozen barrels of a toxic explosive chemical in an Iowa munitions plant on Wednesday, despite public outcry over the potential health impacts on neighboring communities and an ongoing legal battle. Nearly five tons of degraded lead azide, a chemical compound used as a detonator in cartridges and shells, are set to be detonated at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, a city in Des Moines County of nearly 400 people some 13 km away from the Mississippi River separating the state from Illinois. On Nov. 19, Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle posted on social media that discussions with environmental officials and the local community determined a controlled detonation of the lead azide stockpile “posed the lowest risk to the public in the immediate and surrounding area,” but he announced that the detonation would be postponed from Nov. 20 to Nov. 23. Also on Nov. 19, environmental groups sued the Environmental Protection Agency, which granted the permit to the U.S. Army to carry out the detonation, and a federal appeals court ordered a temporary freeze on the permit. Then, on Nov. 21, the Justice Department said it plans to use emergency powers to avoid the permit requirement for detonation. On Nov. 22, the Army rescheduled the blast for Nov. 25, saying that the new time would “allow for more optimal weather conditions and all mitigation measures to be emplaced.” Environmental groups have argued that the U.S. Army is “ sidestepping ” the judicial process. They claim that the EPA approved the detonation plan without enough public notice and without thoroughly studying alternatives. The detonation risks community exposure to lead, a neurotoxin health officials have long documented to cause a variety of health problems in pregnant women and children. There is no safe exposure level to lead: exposed children can suffer damage to the brain and nervous system, learning and behavioral issues, speech and hearing impairments, while pregnant women face increased risks of premature births and miscarriages. The Federal Aviation Administration has restricted flights around Middletown from Monday through Wednesday. Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds activated a state emergency operations center on Nov. 20. In neighboring Illinois, officials argued that they are similarly at risk from airborne lead-containing particles the detonation will produce. On Sunday, Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker said he spoke with the Army, the EPA, and other agencies about the planned detonation, adding that he was “continuing to press for the release of more public information to help keep Illinoisans safe.” “The Army has clearly mishandled this situation, and Iowans and residents in our neighboring states deserve a full review of all of the missteps that led us to this point,” said Wally Taylor, attorney for the environmental organization Sierra Club’s Iowa chapter, one of the petitioners against the EPA. “However, if detonation is now the only option, it is imperative that everyone impacted has access to the full range of testing, mitigation, and remediation resources.” Why is the Army choosing to detonate the stockpile? In March, during what the Army said was a “routine stockpile surveillance operation” at the 19,000-acre plant, technicians discovered 68 drums of degraded lead azide in underground concrete bunkers, which it said had potentially become unstable. The barrels have languished underground for nearly two decades, and the Army said moving the chemical off-site for disposal would risk accidental detonation. Between April and September 2026, the EPA issued three emergency storage permits so the Army could continue storing the stockpile safely while the Army assessed how to treat it. In its environmental assessment , the Army concluded that doing nothing would create “a constant threat of an accidental, unmitigated detonation,” which would have “significant, uncontrolled adverse impacts.” But while detonating the stockpile on-site would “produce severe, instantaneous physical effects” such as blast overpressure and noise and would locally release hazardous materials such as lead particulates and combustion gases in the short term, the Army says these impacts are “heavily mitigated.” Justine Barati, a public affairs specialist for the Army Sustainment Command, told a local news station on Nov. 18 that the Army’s window to safely dispose of the stockpiles was narrowing as winter is arriving. Barati said colder weather or disturbances could cause the stockpiles to detonate spontaneously. “We’re trying to do a controlled detonation to minimize the impact to the community and the environment,” Barati said. “This is not something that we take lightly. We know that this is a disruption to people and that is not our intent, but we’re trying to do this in the safest manner possible.” On Nov. 21, the New York Times reported that, in late March, the Army had initially awarded a contract to MuniRem Environmental, a Georgia-based company that would neutralize the stockpile using chemicals. But two months later, it canceled the deal over purported safety concerns. The EPA granted an emergency permit to detonate the stockpiles between Nov. 13, 2026 and Feb. 11, 2027. The permit for the on-site detonation echoed the risk linked with alternative means of disposal, saying that “recrystallization of the lead azide during long-term storage has increased the material’s sensitivity to friction and shock, creating a highly unstable and dangerous situation.” In the Army’s public notice issued just days before the initial blast schedule , it said the lead azide barrels will be detonated in two, rapid-fire shots inside concrete, earth-covered magazines surrounded by Hesco barriers filled with sand about two stories high. Before and during the detonation, the soil above the magazines will be saturated with water, and water misters will be spraying, all in an attempt to control the amount of lead that could travel through the air beyond the plant. The notice added that models projected the level of lead particles in the air after the detonation “may be elevated but well below the level at which EPA would require protective actions be taken.” What’s the legal battle about? Iowa Environmental Council and the Sierra Club, both nonprofit environmental advocacy organizations, sought to suspend the EPA permit. In a suit filed before the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit, the plaintiffs argued that the permit authorized the Army to detonate the lead azide “in the open,” adding that the blast would create “a plume of lead dust that will blanket homes and communities” possibly as far as 100 mi or more. The petitioners argued that the Army did not promptly and accurately inform the public of the detonation and its impact. The Army said it had informed the local community ahead of the planned blast, including at an open house at the Army Reserve Center in mid-October, but the petitioners argued many residents and local officials claimed to only have learned of the planned detonation “through friends and social media.” The petitioners also emphasized how there’s no safe level of exposure to lead. The court sided with the petitioners and granted the emergency stay on Nov. 19 pending the ruling. But in its Nov. 21 filing to the court, the Justice Department said it would use emergency powers allowing the Army to continue with the blast without an environmental permit, citing federal exemptions. The department emphasized the “immediate risk” posed by the stockpile, while saying that the Army “intends to act consistent with the terms of the Emergency Permit and its mitigation measures even if not in effect.” Thien Chau, an attorney for Earthjustice, which helped sue the EPA, said in a statement that “despite claiming public safety is its top priority and public communication is essential to trust, the Army seemed more concerned over the weekend with finding a way to sidestep the judicial process than on meeting the public’s demands for greater transparency, notice to affected communities, and far stronger protection of people, property, and the environment from serious harm.” What’s the anticipated impact of the detonation? While safety measures will be fully enforced, the Army said in its public notice that during the detonation, it anticipates ground vibration and a dust plume that spreads “some lead-containing particles” in the air, which will deposit on the ground. The notice said Middletown residents can expect the plume to linger for no more than an hour, depending on wind speed. The Army advised residents to evacuate and avoid the affected area in Iowa, and urged those who could not leave to stay indoors, close windows and doors, and turn off heating and ​cooling systems that could bring in outside air. It also said residents should wet-clean surfaces to remove lead dust. Precautionary measures were not limited to Iowa: In Illinois, agriculture officials recommended ways to protect livestock and pets, including keeping animals indoors until the plume passes, and their rigorous washing afterward. Amid this, several politicians continued to express concern over the risks ahead of the continued detonation. U.S. Senator-elect Josh Turek of Iowa posted on social media Sunday that he believes that a full investigation is needed not only into the stockpile’s prolonged unsafe treatment and why safer methods of disposal are needed, but also into “what other potentially dangerous materials are being stored at [the plant] and their condition, and what procedures are needed to ensure this never happens again.” Turek as well as a group of Illinois Democrats—U.S. Senators Dick Durbin and Tammy Duckworth; Lieutenant Governor and U.S. Senator-elect Juliana Stratton; U.S. Rep. Eric Sorensen; and Gov. Pritzker—and two Illinois Republicans, Representatives Darin LaHood and Mary Miller, sent a letter to acting Army Secretary Telle and EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin on Nov. 19 expressing their grave concerns over the planned detonation, calling to postpone it. The potential health risk caused by the detonation threatens Iowa, which is already suffering from having one of the highest cancer incidences in the U.S. “Because of the decisions that have already been made over the course of months, if not years, no good options exist and the situation is more dangerous and unpredictable than it ever should have been,” Rob Sand, who’s set to take office as Iowa’s new governor in January, posted Sunday. “Iowans deserve transparency over how we got here, then answers and accountability to stop this from ever happening again.”

items.author: Marisa Kendall
items.title: What it took for 5 Californians to pull themselves out of homelessness
items.summary: On the surface, California’s homelessness crisis often seems unsurmountable: Tents and RVs line city streets and nearly 180,000 people have nowhere to call home. But every year, thousands of Californians successfully claw their way out of homelessness . Each person’s story of how they did it is unique, influenced by what led them there in the first place, their individual needs and their past traumas. CalMatters interviewed five Californians who have survived homelessness and come out the other side, and we are sharing those stories here as examples of interventions that can work. Some common themes flow through them, showing that housing, while crucial, isn’t always enough. People need a reason to keep going – a passion such as music, helping others, or spirituality – and a community to support them and keep them accountable. ‘Let them grow together’ John Janosko depended on his friends and community during the years he lived in Oakland’s largest homeless encampment. “That’s what kept me sane,” he said. “Because those are the ones who understand you the most.” When city workers tore down the camp in 2023, they offered Janosko and many of his friends something unusual: the chance to stay together and move as a group into temporary tiny homes . That opportunity meant he could lean on his community as he transitioned back into mainstream society after nearly a decade of homelessness. Now, at 58, he has his own apartment, is sober and dedicates his time to helping other people who are homeless. John Janosko, 58, who was previously unhoused for ten years, at his apartment in Oakland on Aug. 28, 2026. Photo by Sarahbeth Maney for CalMatters Janosko’s time on the streets, which he refers to as an “adventure,” started in 2013, when he lost his job and apartment after struggling with an addiction to crack cocaine, and later methamphetamine. Around 2019 he helped launch the Wood Street camp, which grew to more than 300 occupants. Residents fashioned make-shift amenities including an outdoor kitchen, shower and community clothing closet, hosted parties and protests, launched a GoFundMe and started a registered nonprofit. Janosko was a driving force behind it all, and he thrived on it. But Janosko, who’d recently had a heart attack, knew he couldn’t live there forever. The city of Oakland and Caltrans were making it increasingly clear that the campers were no longer welcome. So when the city offered to move him and several dozen of his friends into new tiny homes down the street, he agreed. The miniscule unit, big enough for a cot and a mini fridge, was a stepping stone that helped Janosko get ready for independent living. He got re-accustomed to having the privacy of a locked door. He started taking culinary classes and settled into a regular schedule. “It was the stability I needed,” he said. John Janosko shows old photographs from his time being unhoused that hang on a wall in his apartment in Oakland on Aug. 28, 2026. Photo by Sarahbeth Maney for CalMatters An obvious pitfall of tiny homes , which have gained popularity recently as a solution to homelessness, is that while they’re supposed to be temporary, occupants often can’t find permanent housing once they leave. Janosko estimates fewer than half of his Wood Street friends secured permanent housing after the tiny homes. He was one of the lucky ones. In 2024, after about a year in the tiny home, he found a subsidized apartment where he now pays $258 a month in rent using his Social Security income. Part of it was chance: Janosko thinks having a heart attack placed him at a higher priority in the county’s housing queue. But the support of his Wood Street friends also helped keep him from getting discouraged along the way, he said. It’s common for people living in encampments to form close bonds with their street families, and people sometimes become isolated and depressed when moved alone out of those communities and into shelters or housing. Some programs try to account for that by keeping street communities together – such as Los Angeles’ Inside Safe program, which moves entire encampments into hotels. But it’s not the norm. John Janosko opens a photo book of childhood memories from growing up in the Bay Area, at his apartment in Oakland on Aug. 28, 2026. His adoptive parents gave Janosko the book after he experienced homelessness. Photo by Sarahbeth Maney for CalMatters To Janosko, it’s an obvious solution. “Keep them together,” he said. “Let them grow together. They do better that way. Don’t dismantle everything that they know.” From overdose to accountability Ifalayo Harper’s third try at sobriety, during her 11th year of homelessness, was the one that worked. That’s because this time, when she finished rehab in 2023, there was something different waiting for her on the other side. She moved into a unique, self-governed sober-housing community with two dozen formerly homeless people called Homefulness . “There’s always somebody to keep me accountable,” said Harper, 43. The other key to her success is her faith: She embraced traditional Yoruba religious practices during a trip to Nigeria in the midst of her recovery. Ifalayo Harper inside her apartment at the Homefulness community in Oakland on Sept. 14, 2026. Photo by Anna Hoch-Kenney, CalMatters Harper, whose birth name is LeaJay, became homeless in 2012, after her drinking cost her her job, and then her home. Once on the street, she started using methamphetamine, then heroin, and then fentanyl, getting sucked deeper and deeper into addiction. Like Janosko, Harper lived in the Wood Street encampment. But while that camp was a lifeline for him, Harper’s relationship with it was more fraught: The camp made it far too easy for her to get drugs. So when the city cleared the encampment, it was “bittersweet,” Harper said. The city moved Harper and her RV to a city-sanctioned “safe parking lot” all the way across town. It was isolating, but it gave her the nudge she needed to start thinking seriously about recovery. Two months later, Harper overdosed in the backseat of her college-age daughter’s car after injecting a shot of fentanyl into her neck. When she woke up in the hospital, her friend, Homefulness founder Lisa “Tiny” Gray-Garcia, offered to get her into rehab. After that, Harper moved into Homefulness in December 2023. She recently got a job in the same San Francisco drug treatment program where she was a patient three years ago. Unlike other homeless housing programs, Homefulness has no nonprofit setting rules for residents and no government funding. Residents decide things as a group and take turns doing chores that include feeding the chickens and goat. There’s no rent. Residents contribute toward utilities and other group expenses if they can, but no one pays more than $300 a month, and most pay less, if anything. First: Ifalayo Harper spends a moment with Cappuccino the goat during a stroll around the Oakland Homefulness community. Last: Ifalayo Harper makes jewelry in the attic of her apartment, which she transformed into a creative workshop. It is her favorite part of her apartment and where she spends hours sewing and beading. Harper, who was previously unhoused for years, said making jewelry helped when she was going through recovery. Photos by Anna Hoch-Kenney, CalMatters It’s a novel – even radical – approach, but it’s slowly gaining momentum. In addition to the East Oakland property where Harper lives, Gray-Garcia and her group own a second lot down the street where they’ve built two tiny homes and plan to add 12 more, and a third lot in San Francisco where they’re planning a four-story building. The group also is raising money for sites in Los Angeles and Washington. By and large, the people who have moved in, stay. Many of them are people who have been labeled hard to help, or “service resistant,” by society. Gray-Garcia says the reason it works is simple: community. “We need each other,” she said. “We don’t need to be alone in a room with a door and a lock and a key. That’s not a human way to live, at all.” Help from a stranger After more than a decade of methamphetamine use and homelessness, Mike McCarthy figured eventually he would die on the streets. “I got tired of the lifestyle,” McCarthy said. “It got old after a while. I just kept begging for help, kept praying: ‘I want out. I want help. I don’t want this anymore.’” Then he met Jennifer Su. Mike McCarthy, 36, at Jennifer Su’s home in Pacheco, on Aug. 21, 2026. McCarthy overcame addiction and currently lives with Su. Photo by Sarahbeth Maney for CalMatters At the time McCarthy was sleeping at a camp in Pleasant Hill, an upper-middle class suburb in Contra Costa County, and Su often stopped by to visit her own son, who was also homeless. She and McCarthy made an unlikely pair. He’s a 36-year-old tattooed metal music fan. She’s a 57-year-old county government employee who’s active in her church. One day, Su asked McCarthy if he could use some help. She took him to the DMV to get an ID card. She helped him sign up for public assistance benefits, Medi-Cal, and, eventually, addiction treatment. When he initially got assigned to an outpatient treatment program – meaning he’d have to try and get sober while living in a tent during a winter of torrential rain – she pushed to get him reassigned to in-patient treatment. When he got admitted to a program that didn’t allow pets, Su took in his beloved pitbull mix, Rose. McCarthy graduated from the program in January 2025 and moved into a sober living home. But conditions at the home were challenging. He slept in a bunk bed in a room he shared with three other men, and there were strict rules about chores and possessions. Mike McCarthy and Jennifer Su at her home in Pacheco on Aug. 21, 2026. Photo by Sarahbeth Maney for CalMatters In July 2025, Su offered McCarthy a spare bedroom in her own home in Pacheco, which she shares with her husband and dogs. McCarthy accepted. Now, he pays rent when he can and helps with chores, including cleaning the bathroom and picking up after the dogs. He got a job at the Safeway he used to sleep behind, he’s working toward getting his GED and he plays guitar in a band that just had its first gig in Berkeley. His passion for music is a major reason he stays sober, McCarthy said – he knows if he started using again, he’d be out of the band. And, he doesn’t want to disappoint Su. For Su, each of McCarthy’s successes have been a balm to her heart. She’s been trying for years to help her own son, who has schizophrenia, uses methamphetamine and has been in and out of psychiatric facilities. But like so many people who love someone with a serious mental illness, she’s found that getting him the treatment he needs often seems impossible. When she felt like she’d failed her son, McCarthy helped her see it wasn’t her fault. Where she couldn’t help her son, she could help McCarthy. “It was really healing for me,” Su said, “and just a blessing in my life to see him doing so well.” Her own son recently went into residential treatment, but she continues to worry about how long he’ll stay there and what will happen to him once he gets out. McCarthy believes he’d still be on the street without Su. “I just don’t think I would have been able to do it on my own,” he said. “I pretty much needed somebody to help me get out of there.” Mike McCathy plays the guitar at Jennifer Su’s home in Pacheco, on Aug. 21, 2026. Photo by Sarahbeth Maney for CalMatters While McCarthy’s story proves recovery is possible, it also highlights how difficult it is to navigate the system without someone like Su. Su believes her relationship with McCarthy could be an example. What if programs matched their unhoused clients with housed families to guide them back into society, helping with everything from going to the DMV to filing taxes? “You don’t just…put a roof over someone’s head and expect that they’ll be able to thrive,” Su said. “People have to have a reason to live. People have to have things that they enjoy, and friendships.” Crowdsourcing an apartment Judy Cleborne was in her 70s, feeling unsafe after multiple break-ins to her RV, when she decided she couldn’t keep spending her nights parked on the street in San Diego. That was in 2024. This year, she finally sold her RV and moved into her own apartment. But when she embarked on her journey to find housing, she had no idea how long, frustrating, and at times she says “soul-destroying,” that process would be. She got help from Dawn Contreras, a case manager with the nonprofit PATH, who would eventually find her an apartment. Judy Cleborne in her new apartment in San Diego on Oct. 5, 2026. Cleborne got into housing this year after living out of her RV for several years. Photo by Zoë Meyers for CalMatters The search was slow at first. Between the two of them, Contreras and Cleborne called more than three-dozen properties with no luck. Even in low-rent buildings, Cleborne’s income was a barrier – she received about $1,650 a month in Social Security. And competition was sky-high. “Just when you think you’ve found a perfect spot, they’re like, ‘nope, we’re not taking anybody today, call this place,’” Contreras said. “And you call, and they’re like, ‘nope our waitlist is long.’” Cleborne got a job at Goodwill to boost her income and give herself a better chance at qualifying for an apartment. At the same time, Contreras was consulting her secret weapon – a group chat of other caseworkers who shared tips and resources. Someone in the chat knew of a building that had an opening, and Contreras pounced. Cleborne moved in this past March. Judy Cleborne was able to decorate her new apartment in San Diego with the help of Humble Design. Cleborne got into housing this year after living out of her RV for several years. Photo by Zoë Meyers for CalMatters It’s not uncommon for it to take a year or longer for her clients to find housing, Contreras said. They sometimes get so discouraged that they lose hope. Trauma from years of homelessness also often erodes people’s ability to persevere through numerous rejections. And not everyone has a Contreras in their corner. Today, Cleborne’s struggles aren’t over. She’s using a rapid rehousing voucher to cover part of her rent, which is set to expire in January. Then, she’ll have to start paying the entire $1,550 a month herself. “It’s a big rent payment, and I have a car payment, and it’s all scary,” Cleborne said. “But that’s my challenge, to make it all work.” A forced choice: Jail or treatment? James Presley’s pathway to recovery and housing started in a jail cell. Presley, who has been diagnosed with schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, was sleeping on benches in Santa Monica, hearing and seeing things that weren’t there, when he was arrested in 2025 on a breaking and entering charge. He says he biked to his grandmother’s house, where he’d lived before she kicked him out, broke in through a back window, and laid down on the bed in his old room. When he woke up the next morning, the police were there. For someone who is unhoused and has a serious mental illness, an arrest often starts a vicious cycle of jumping between jail and the street. But 31-year-old Presley was selected for a program by Los Angeles County’s Office of Diversion and Reentry, which gives people the option of completing mental health treatment instead of jail. Presley graduated from the program in May, and moved into an apartment last month. He’s no longer experiencing hallucinations, or using alcohol or marijuana. “My mind is clear,” Presley said. “Plus, I’m sober. So it helped a lot.” James Presley at his new apartment in Los Angeles on Oct. 17, 2026. Photo by Alisha Jucevic for CalMatters Presley spent about a month in jail before he was accepted into the diversion program and started a six-month in-patient hospital stay. Then he moved into a halfway house with about 20 other men also participating in diversion programs. Presley doesn’t believe he would have chosen to enter treatment if he hadn’t faced time in jail. That’s true of many program participants, said Dr. Clemens Hong, who leads the county’s diversion programs. “The big piece, though, is: Can we treat them long enough and successfully enough to allow them to understand the benefits of treatment beyond staying out of jail?” he said. “That’s what leads to the ultimate success of the program…I think we achieve that in a lot of folks.” To qualify for diversion, participants must be homeless, have a serious mental illness, and be charged with a crime. The idea is to catch people who have fallen through the holes in all the other safety nets. A judge orders them into treatment, and in some programs, can also order them to take medication. Each person’s treatment plan includes housing and other services tailored to their individual needs. James Presley in the courtyard of his new apartment in Los Angeles on Oct. 17, 2026. After four years on a waiting list for Section 8 housing, he moved into the apartment in mid-October. Presley is now working on getting furniture and setting up his new home. He said he is celebrating two years clean and sober and feeling positive about this new chapter. Photo by Alisha Jucevic for CalMatters The 11-year-old diversion program is similar in some ways to the state’s newer CARE Court , which uses the courts to place people with severe mental illnesses into treatment. Unlike CARE Court, where participants have not necessarily been charged with a crime, the diversion program has the teeth to force participants to comply with their treatment plans. The average diversion participant has been incarcerated 10 times before starting the program. After entering diversion, 56% don’t go back to jail in two years, and some never go back, Hong said. That means the program helps more than half of participants turn their lives around, which Hong called a very high success rate. Last month, Presley moved into a one-bedroom apartment in Los Angeles’ Silver Lake neighborhood. He has a Section 8 housing voucher, which means he pays a third of his Social Security income in rent and the rest is subsidized by the voucher. It’s been a long time coming. Presley spent four years on the waitlist for a voucher before he got to the top of the queue. He also serves on the “lived experience board” for the county’s Office of Diversion and Reentry, where he finds fulfillment by suggesting improvements to the programs he once belonged to – his way of helping others who are on their recovery journey. “I feel like I’m balanced,” Presley said. “I feel good. I feel like I accomplished a lot and came a long way.” This story was made possible in part by support from The James Irvine Foundation.

items.originalTitle: How to talk to kids, according to kids
items.author: Allie Volpe
items.title: How to talk to kids, according to kids
items.summary: Nine-year-old Leo is attempting to share his screen with me over FaceTime for a very important reason: I must hear an extremely funny sound — the clang of a metal pipe hitting the ground . The mere act of pulling up the YouTube video causes our call to glitch and we’re forced to reconnect. With the technical difficulties sorted, I do admit the sound is funny in an exaggerated, cartoonish way. But why does this crash in particular, this specific clip, tickle his funny bone? “Because if it annoys mommy enough, it’s funny,” Leo told me. This conversation with Leo was one of several I had recently with kids between the ages of 6 and 11 where I asked them on how they like to have fun and with whom. I don’t consider myself adept at making small talk with anyone under the age of 20, mainly because I’m hardly around any such people. Most of my friends don’t have little ones and at family parties, I smile politely at my cousins’ kids from afar. My attempts at conversation with the youth feel strained and awkward opposed to snappy and light, so I figured this assignment would be good practice. Chances are, you know some kids — a friend’s toddler, a relative’s tween — and might need a little guidance, too. When I asked Leo whether the adults in his life could be better at interacting with children, he cut me off. “This adult particularly?” he said, gesturing to his mother, just off camera. “No, she is perfect. Other adults in general, maybe.” As more adults choose not to have kids , or wait later in life to do so , it’s entirely possible you, like me, don’t spend a ton of time with small humans and can’t remember what it was like to be one. What do they even like? How do you keep their attention? How do you avoid saying the wrong thing? Figuring this out is important given that intergenerational relationships are a net positive for both adults and kids : Grown-ups get the chance to learn from the young people in their lives and, in turn, children soak in older generations’ knowledge and wisdom. Plus, if most of us agree “it takes a village” when it comes to raising kids, it’s worth trying to be good villagers. So I decided to ask the experts: Kids themselves. From my conversations, I’ve distilled a few do’s and don’ts for how to have better conversations with kids. Find some common ground (animals are a safe bet) In nearly every one of my conversations, children mentioned caring about, thinking about, or being interested in, animals. “If [grown-ups] just want to be my friend, maybe they could introduce them[selves] to me and tell [me] what their favorite animal is, and then maybe I’ll get used to them and then I start liking them better,” Logan, 9, told me. Kids seem especially primed to enjoy wildlife. In one study, when children were presented with the option of interacting with toys or animals, they consistently chose animals. Animals are varied and visually engaging , giving kids plenty to be fascinated with. Logan and her 6-year-old sister Apple play a 20 questions-style game called “guess the animal.” The trickiest animal she’s offered clues for was a gila monster. “It’s kind of like a lizard and it’s flat. It’s like a reptile and it’s orange and black,” Logan said. Even if you don’t have a lot to say in the creature department, try to find some commonality. The key is to pay attention to what kids seem genuinely curious about and to invite them into your world — or to try to get an invite to theirs. Eleven-year-old Eli’s interests range from history and war reenactments to Legos and Call of Duty. Some of the adults in his life leveraged these subject areas and have found common ground: He connects with his uncle over a shared love of outdoorsy adventures, and a few neighbors over their historic cars and the military. Do an activity together It should come as no surprise that kids like to do stuff, as opposed to boring adults who mostly like to talk. Seven-year-old Winona introduced herself as “a kid with a lot of energy,” which means she loves to play tag and hide-and-seek — an activity one of her aunts is happy to partake in whenever she visits. “If I had a world and it was called Winnieland, every adult would play with me,” Winona told me. “We would ride roller coasters. We would play tag. And what’s my favorite thing? My favorite thing is, oh, I know: obstacle courses and haunted houses.” Leo, too, thinks it’s easier to connect with adults when you’re doing something together, like playing a video game. His tia is one of the best Mario Kart players he’s ever seen. Nothing lights up 8-year-old Hugo quite like soccer. I sensed some initial hesitation when we spoke, but any time our meandering chat came back to the sport, he suddenly had much more to say. (He’s on three teams, according to his mom.) Kicking around a ball is a great way to bond with him. Adults could be more interesting to kids, Hugo said, if they didn’t work so much, if they didn’t have so much to do. “My friends are always active, and my parents are always doing stuff,” he said. Activity-based bonding, like singing, telling stories, and reading to children, promotes positive social-emotional development in kids , according to research. Families with school-aged kids who engage in physical activity together had improved cohesion, per another study. Doing an activity or playing a game removes the pressure to keep the conversation going — you can simply talk about the thing in front of you, and it’s okay to sit in silence for a couple minutes while you color if you can’t think of anything to say. Get a little playful Aside from her parents, a few of Logan’s favorite adults to interact with are her teacher and teacher’s assistant. What makes her TA especially skilled at connecting with children is her ability to imagine and play, Logan said. One day at recess, Logan and a friend took turns trying on the TA’s lanyard, pretending they were in charge. Rather than shut them down, the TA upped the ante: “She said that she was going to steal the principal’s name tag and say that she was the principal,” Logan said. Logan’s preferred form of play involves dreaming up new universes and games and when grown-ups can join in and play pretend, all the better. Getting on kids’ wavelength might mean suspending disbelief, too. Winona told me that when she was younger, she had an imaginary friend named Christopher, a raccoon who was prone to making a mess. If connecting with a kid means referring to a fake racoon by name, it’s a conversational path worth taking. All the kids I talked to seemed to notice and appreciate when adults are down to play — when they don’t rationalize make-believe scenarios and logic, and instead lean into silliness. Make a point to turn off your adult brain and try asking questions about their imaginary friend or what the castle the queen of their dream universe lives in looks like; basically, just say “ yes, and… ” Just be normal Perhaps my biggest faux pas when talking to children, I’ve learned, is treating them like aliens whose world I will never understand. In reporting this story, I learned that the things kids say they value when interacting with others are largely the same for grown-ups, too. What to avoid when talking to kids Don’t play tricks on them or elide the truth: Logan and Apple’s mom told them they were going to “a special place” which turned out to be the library — a locale Apple did not find very special. While not technically a lie, she felt duped. “I don’t think the library is a special place because I don’t really like to read,” Apple said. Don’t make it all about you: Leo finds it particularly annoying when he tries to talk to an adult about something that interests him and grown-ups bring the conversation back to their life. “It’s not all about you,” he said. Don’t freak them out about the future, or bring up sensitive topics that might make them feel awkward: “Since I’m around that age, I don’t really like it when people talk about me changing and having puberty and not getting along with my friends as much,” Logan said. Don’t use a loud voice: Both Leo and Logan agreed they get scared when adults raise their voices. Don’t be discouraged if a kid doesn’t open up to you immediately. You’re unfamiliar and that can perhaps be scary or intimidating! They’re comfortable chatting with their parents, but generally take a little more time warming up to other grown-ups. And familiarity is key: Those I talked to mentioned their teachers, relatives, neighbors, and parents’ friends as being their favorite adults. Regardless of your level of closeness, treat a kid much like you would treat any other person. Kids want to feel acknowledged and listened to. Eli remembered a friend’s mom ignoring him when he greeted her. “She didn’t want to talk and it was just weird. It was awkward,” he said. “I felt like I’m being ghosted.” So look them in the eye, respond appropriately when they tell you sad or exciting news, and ask follow-up questions. They notice when you’re not paying attention or when you put them off. “Kids always say, ‘Come on, let’s go play. Come on, let’s go play.’ But adults are like, ‘We’ll play later,’” Winona said. So make an effort to engage with them, if only briefly. They can also tell when you’re making things too simplistic. “That makes me want to rage,” Eli said. So treat them with (age-appropriate) respect. But perhaps most importantly, they do not want to be told to do chores. Luckily for you, a person who is not their parent, you don’t have to.
